insights.title: Read the experience line, not just the title
insights.text: Some adverts called "Data Analyst" or "Data Analyst I" asked for 3 to 8 years of experience. Look for intern, graduate, apprentice, junior or associate roles, or use "You vs a job advert" to check the level.

insights.title: Big graduate schemes hire for potential
insights.text: Several UK graduate schemes and apprenticeships (banks, media, the NHS) mostly ask for problem solving, communication and care over detail, and test them with numerical reasoning tests and case studies. Many accept any degree subject.

insights.title: Remote entry-level roles are scarce
insights.text: Remote junior data roles genuinely open to Africa were the hardest to find. African employers (banks, telcos, NGOs, consultancies, startups) and international internships (for example UN agencies) are the most realistic first step.

insights.title: Check visa and location rules
insights.text: Many US roles do not sponsor visas or need US security clearance; some UK schemes sponsor visas and some do not. Check before you spend time on an application.

insights.title: French is an advantage
insights.text: Several West African and international roles asked for French. If you speak it, put it clearly on your CV.

insights.title: Employers expect you to use AI tools well
insights.text: About a third of US and UK adverts mentioned using AI tools responsibly. Using them openly and checking their work, as this program asks, is the habit they want.

sql.example: Monzo keeps its data in a BigQuery data warehouse and turns raw app events into clean tables with dbt, a tool where the work is written in SQL. In 2021 the project had over 4,700 data models and about 600,000 lines of SQL, written not only by data staff but also by software engineers and business analysts. SQL is the shared language that lets many teams build on the same trusted tables.
sql.source_title: An introduction to Monzo's data stack (Monzo blog, 2021)

sql.example: Airbnb created its own internal 'Data University' because general online courses did not match its own data and tools. Middle-level classes taught SQL and Superset (a dashboard tool), and helped some non-technical staff take on project manager roles. After the launch, weekly use of internal data tools rose from 30% to 45% of staff.
sql.source_title: Airbnb is running its own internal university to teach data science (TechCrunch, 2017)

sql.example: A business analyst at Moniepoint, who first worked mostly with spreadsheets and customer feedback, was introduced to SQL by her manager. She learned by taking online courses and reading the team's internal queries, and in less than a year she became a Data Analyst. She now uses data to track loan repayment behaviour and to find reconciliation problems, for example when a supermarket's books and Moniepoint's system show different results.
sql.source_title: Curiosity Killed The Cat? Thankfully, I'm A Data Analyst! (Moniepoint Blog)

spreadsheets.example: In 2020, Public Health England pulled COVID-19 test results into Excel templates saved in the old XLS format, which can hold only about 65,000 rows. Each test result used several rows, so each file could hold only about 1,400 cases, and 15,841 positive cases were missed from the reports, which delayed contact tracing. The lesson for analysts: know the limits of your tool and always check that row counts match.
spreadsheets.source_title: Excel: Why using Microsoft's tool caused Covid-19 results to be lost (BBC News, 2020)

spreadsheets.company: Nigeria Federal Ministry of Health and NPHCDA
spreadsheets.example: Until 2014, Nigeria's immunisation programme collected vaccine data with an Excel-based WHO tool. Users reported data entry errors, no access to past data, a one-month delay between collection and analysis, and reports that did not match between health facilities and local government areas. So the government asked partners to build an online routine immunisation module and dashboard in DHIS2.
spreadsheets.source_title: Implementing the routine immunisation data module and dashboard of DHIS2 in Nigeria, 2014-2019 (via PubMed Central)

spreadsheets.example: UK government statisticians publish many official data tables as spreadsheets. The Government Analysis Function wrote guidance called 'Releasing statistics in spreadsheets' for everyone who publishes data tables this way. Its aim is to make these spreadsheets more usable, more accessible and more machine readable (easy for software to read).
spreadsheets.source_title: Releasing statistics in spreadsheets (Government Analysis Function)

python.example: Netflix says many of its teams build their tools mainly in Python. For example, one team uses Python libraries such as numpy, scipy and pandas to automatically analyse thousands of related signals when an alert shows a problem. Netflix staff are also heavy users of Jupyter notebooks, and an experimentation team is building a platform for scientists and engineers to analyse A/B tests.

Spotify built Luigi, a free Python package for building pipelines of batch jobs: tasks that must run in order, such as load the data, then clean it, then make a report. Spotify says it uses Luigi internally to run thousands of tasks every day.

python.company: Bluesquare / OpenHEXA (used with ministries of health in Africa)
python.example: OpenHEXA is an open-source public health data platform from Bluesquare. Data scientists write Jupyter notebooks in Python or R to explore and analyse data, and they build automatic data pipelines. In Niger, Bluesquare and national teams used it to produce automatic monthly immunisation performance reports at national, regional and district level.
python.source_title: OpenHEXA: open-source, collaborative data integration and analysis platform for public health

statistics.company: DHIS2 (health information software used by many ministries of health)
statistics.example: DHIS2's Data Quality app has an Outlier Detection tool that flags unusual values in health facility data. It can compare each value with the mean (Z-score), with the median (modified Z-score), or with stored minimum and maximum values. The guide warns that the mean and standard deviation method is only right for normally distributed data: data with big seasonal changes can create false alarms.

statistics.company: AHADI and partners, SNT Code Library (malaria data, Sierra Leone teaching example)
statistics.example: Analysts who supported malaria planning in more than 30 countries share their code in the SNT Code Library, using Sierra Leone routine data as a teaching example. It compares three ways to find outliers in each health facility's monthly case counts: mean +/- 2 standard deviations, median +/- 2.5 MAD, and the interquartile range (IQR). It explains that the mean is pulled by extreme values, that facility malaria data is often right-skewed, and that seasonal peaks and real outbreaks must not be 'corrected' by mistake.
statistics.source_title: Outlier detection methods (Community Code Library for Subnational Tailoring of Malaria Interventions)

statistics.example: Some Netflix datasets grow by more than 10 billion records a day, so the company needed automatic outlier detection to protect data quality. Simple methods such as moving averages with standard deviations were not robust enough, partly because the data is not always normally distributed and has hourly, weekly and monthly seasonal patterns. Netflix built and open-sourced a more robust tool called RAD.
statistics.source_title: RAD - Outlier Detection on Big Data (Netflix Technology Blog, 2015)

data_cleaning.company: Kenya Ministry of Health data (study by Gesicho and colleagues)
data_cleaning.example: Researchers exported eight years (2011-2018) of HIV reporting data from Kenya's national DHIS2 system to Excel: 93,179 facility records from 11,446 health facilities. They screened the data, diagnosed problems and then fixed or removed them: records with no data (50.23%) were removed, and they also found reporting rates above 100% and duplicate facilities. A clean dataset was needed to answer a Ministry of Health question about which facilities report completely and on time.
data_cleaning.source_title: Data cleaning process for HIV-indicator data extracted from DHIS2 national reporting system: a case study of Kenya (BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, 2020)

data_cleaning.example: For Census 2021 in England and Wales, ONS used 'edit rules' to catch impossible answers; for example, a person under 16 cannot have a qualification for census purposes. Missing or inconsistent answers were filled in from similar 'donor' records. About 2.4 million of 26.3 million household records (9%) needed at least one answer filled in this way.
data_cleaning.source_title: Item editing and imputation process for Census 2021, England and Wales (ONS)

data_cleaning.example: To build PesaYetu, a tool that shows Kenyan county budgets, Code for Africa scraped hundreds of data tables from county plan PDFs into a spreadsheet, cleaned them and loaded them into a database. They found that counties reported different things in different ways and that some budget figures did not add up. Cleaning was slow, but it had to happen before counties could be compared fairly.
data_cleaning.source_title: The Covid-19 infodemic: how we fought back with data (Code for Africa)

visualization.example: The BBC News data team built an R package called bbplot and a public 'cookbook' so that charts made with ggplot2 follow the BBC house style. This makes publication-ready graphics easier to repeat and easier for people who are new to R.
visualization.source_title: BBC Visual and Data Journalism cookbook for R graphics

visualization.example: The FT's Visual Journalism team made the 'Visual Vocabulary', a poster and website that help journalists choose the best chart for what the data needs to show. For example, to show values above and below a reference point (like a trade surplus or deficit) it suggests a diverging bar chart. It is the core of newsroom-wide training to improve chart literacy.
visualization.source_title: Financial Times Visual Vocabulary (Financial-Times/chart-doctor on GitHub)

visualization.example: Code for South Africa built Wazimap in 2014 so that journalists could quickly see census and election data for any area as maps and charts, instead of searching long reports and many Excel files. Journalists can embed the visualisations in their stories so readers understand the data at a glance.
visualization.source_title: Code for Africa Builds WaziMap to Make Public Data More User-Friendly for Journalists (ICFJ)

bi_dashboards.example: Superset started at Airbnb in 2015 as a tool to build and explore dashboards, with a no-code chart builder and a SQL editor. Airbnb says it connects SQL analysis with data exploration for thousands of its employees each week. It is now the open-source Apache Superset, also used by companies such as Netflix, Lyft and Dropbox.
bi_dashboards.source_title: The Apache Software Foundation Announces Apache Superset as a Top-Level Project

bi_dashboards.company: Botswana Ministry of Health and Wellness (with UNICEF)
bi_dashboards.example: From 27 March 2020, Botswana ran a COVID-19 tracker in DHIS2, using staff who already had DHIS2 skills. Its dashboard kept a real-time count of COVID-19 numbers, and managers at different levels used it to follow the outbreak and decide on control measures.

bi_dashboards.company: Public Health England (now UK Health Security Agency)
bi_dashboards.example: In 2020 the UK built a COVID-19 dashboard to bring data from more than a dozen sources together in one place, for the public and for leaders in government and health care. It had over 300,000 unique users a day, and about 10,000 people were online at 4pm each day waiting for the update. People even used it to decide whether to visit a friend or go on holiday to an area.
bi_dashboards.source_title: The COVID-19 dashboard: bringing together data and statistics in one place (UKHSA blog, 2020)

communication.example: Since 2003, Uganda's Ministry of Health has produced a District League Table that ranks districts from best to worst using a score built from several indicators, and presents it at national review meetings. A 2018 study found it a convenient way to show many numbers at once, but district managers argued that very different districts should not be compared without taking their differences into account. The lesson: a ranking gets attention, but decision-makers also need the context behind the numbers.
communication.source_title: A critique of the Uganda district league table using a normative health system performance assessment framework (BMC Health Services Research, 2018)

communication.company: Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl, UK)
communication.example: After the 2018 nerve-agent attack in Salisbury, Dstl statisticians designed sampling plans to check which places were safe. They wrote a single document that started with the top-level answer, including 3D images of the plan, and then gave detail for readers who needed it. This let the government advisory group and the military each find what they needed quickly.
communication.source_title: Statistics Under Pressure case study: Salisbury poisonings and decontamination (Royal Statistical Society)

communication.example: During COVID-19, DfT moved from quarterly to daily travel statistics, which were shown at TV press briefings and used by 10 Downing Street and SAGE. To make the numbers easy to compare, the team showed change against a pre-pandemic baseline instead of raw totals, and explained the limits of the data clearly.
communication.source_title: Statistics Under Pressure case study: Transport statistics, shedding light on social distancing during the Covid-19 pandemic (Royal Statistical Society)

ab_testing.example: Netflix puts a random sample of members into a control group (A) that sees the normal service and a treatment group (B) that sees one change, then compares metrics such as engagement. Random assignment keeps everything else equal, so a difference comes from the change and not from something else, like a hit new show. The 'Top 10' rows on Netflix started as an idea that was tested in this way.
ab_testing.source_title: What is an A/B Test? (Netflix Technology Blog, 2021)

ab_testing.example: Booking.com staff write that every change, from full redesigns to bug fixes, is wrapped in an experiment, and that more than a thousand experiments run at the same time. Anyone in the company can search past experiments and their results, so teams learn from earlier successes and failures.
ab_testing.source_title: Democratizing online controlled experiments at Booking.com (Kaufman, Pitchforth and Vermeer, 2017)

ab_testing.company: Center for Advanced Hindsight with a mobile health wallet partner (Kenya)
ab_testing.example: A partner sent SMS reminders to users of a mobile health savings wallet. The control message had no savings target; the two test messages had a low target (10 Kenyan shillings) or a high target (100 Kenyan shillings). The low target gave the most people saving and the highest amount saved, which shows how one small change in a message can be tested.
ab_testing.source_title: The SMS Study: Saving for healthcare (Center for Advanced Hindsight)

pandas.example: pandas, the Python library for working with tables of data (DataFrames), started in 2008 at AQR Capital Management, an investment firm, and became open source by the end of 2009. Its mission is to be the basic building block for practical, real-world data analysis in Python.

Man Group, an investment management firm, built ArcticDB, a database that reads and writes pandas DataFrames directly ('Pandas in, Pandas out'). Users can filter, group and create new columns with a pandas-like syntax, which shows how central the DataFrame is to data work in finance.

M-KOPA lists Python, SQL, pandas, numpy and scikit-learn as the tools for its credit data scientists. They analyse repayment data to build models that decide who can get a loan and at what price. M-KOPA says it has helped over 7 million customers access over $2 billion in credit.
pandas.source_title: Senior Data Scientist - Credit Eligibility at M-KOPA (job posting, Shortlist job board)

typical.name: Application and first screen
typical.what_happens: Your CV or form is checked, then you have a 20-30 minute call (or record a video interview) about your background, your motivation and the role.
typical.how_to_prepare: Practise a 1-minute story of who you are, one project you are proud of, and why you want this job.

typical.name: Online test
typical.what_happens: Graduate schemes and large employers often use an online judgement, reasoning or skills test before any interview.
typical.how_to_prepare: Do a few free practice reasoning and situational judgement tests with a timer so the format does not surprise you.

typical.name: Technical interview
typical.what_happens: A data person asks technical questions or works through a problem with you, for example SQL, statistics or code you wrote.
typical.how_to_prepare: Practise solving small SQL and statistics problems while you explain each step out loud.

typical.name: Take-home task
typical.what_happens: You get a dataset or small problem to work on at home, and often send back slides or code that you discuss later.
typical.how_to_prepare: Keep your work tidy, write down your assumptions, and finish with a clear answer and a recommendation.

typical.name: Case study
typical.what_happens: Interviewers describe a real business problem and ask how you would use data to solve it; it feels more like a conversation than a test.
typical.how_to_prepare: Practise a simple structure: check the question, choose metrics, say what data you need, then give a recommendation.

typical.name: Presentation of findings
typical.what_happens: You present your analysis (of a dataset they give you, or of your take-home task) to a panel and answer questions.
typical.how_to_prepare: Start with your main finding in one sentence, use 2-3 simple charts, and practise answering 'why?' and 'so what?'.

typical.name: Behavioural / competency interview
typical.what_happens: Questions about how you worked with others, solved problems and delivered results, often asked by people outside the data team.
typical.how_to_prepare: Prepare 4-5 real examples using STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) and say what you learned from each.

typical.name: Final round and decision
typical.what_happens: A last interview with the hiring manager or business leaders, then the interviewers meet to agree a decision.
typical.how_to_prepare: Prepare good questions about the team and the work, and be ready to sum up in two sentences why you fit the role.

examples.role: Data Analyst / Data Scientist (all individual-contributor data roles)

stages.name: Recruiter call
stages.what_happens: A 30-minute call about your experience, what you want from a new role, and how the process will work.

stages.name: First-stage call
stages.what_happens: An interviewer asks about the skills on your CV, some behavioural and light technical questions, and asks you to talk through one project you did.

stages.name: Take-home task
stages.what_happens: A role-specific data problem with no time limit; you usually give your answer as a slide deck or presentation.

stages.name: Take-home follow-up (sometimes)
stages.what_happens: A conversation about your solution, your choices, and what you would change if the problem changed.

stages.name: Final interview: case study
stages.what_happens: Interviewers share a real business problem, give you time to think, then you talk through your proposed solution with them.

stages.name: Final interview: collaboration (behavioural)
stages.what_happens: You meet people from outside data, such as a product manager or engineer, and talk about what you delivered, your successes and your challenges.

stages.name: Decision
stages.what_happens: All interviewers meet with the hiring manager, and a 'hiring mentor' reviews the evidence; you usually hear within a week.

examples.source_title: Data Hiring at Monzo - The Interview Process (Monzo blog, 2022)

stages.name: Short questionnaire
stages.what_happens: Selected candidates fill in a short questionnaire.

stages.name: Recruiter screen
stages.what_happens: A screening call with one of GitLab's global recruiters.

stages.name: First interview with a data leader
stages.what_happens: An interview with a leader from the Data team.

stages.name: Team interviews
stages.what_happens: Separate interviews with a Data team member, a business team member and an executive leader.

examples.source_title: Data Analytics job description: Hiring Process (The GitLab Handbook)

examples.role: Data Scientist (data science and analytics roles)

stages.name: Application
stages.what_happens: CV, cover letter and one role-specific question; about half of applicants stop here.

stages.name: Phone screen
stages.what_happens: A 30-minute call with a recruiter about motivation and values, and whether you can explain technical work to a non-technical person.

stages.name: Technical exercise and call
stages.what_happens: You get a simulated dataset and a small working model system, then discuss and improve it with two data scientists in a 45-minute call.

stages.name: Final interview
stages.what_happens: Two one-hour panels, one on people skills and one on technical skills, with questions agreed in advance.

stages.name: Decision meeting
stages.what_happens: The panel meets the hiring manager to agree the final decision.

examples.source_title: Our data science hiring process (FreeAgent engineering blog, 2022)

examples.role: Graduate (Future Talent) programmes, including the Data stream

stages.name: Application form
stages.what_happens: Your details plus free-text questions about you and your motivation.

stages.name: Situational judgement test
stages.what_happens: An online test with work scenarios where you choose what you would do; it checks how well you match the Bank's values.

stages.name: Video interview
stages.what_happens: You record answers to set questions; a person reviews them later.

stages.name: Virtual assessment centre
stages.what_happens: One group exercise and one interview with motivation, behaviour-based and analytical/technical questions (the Bank uses the STARR method).

examples.source_title: How to apply for our Future Talent programmes (Bank of England)

examples.company: UK Government Operational Research Service (Civil Service)
examples.role: Level 6 Data Science Degree Apprenticeship (entry level)

stages.name: Online application form
stages.what_happens: Questions that test the behaviours and technical skills in the Civil Service Success Profiles.

stages.name: Civil Service Judgement Test
stages.what_happens: An online test sent to you after you submit your application.

stages.name: Technical exercise
stages.what_happens: Usually online: a short spoken presentation about a dataset they give you.

stages.name: Interview
stages.what_happens: Questions about how you take charge of your own learning, analyse data and work at pace, alone and in a team.

examples.company: Standard Bank Group (South Africa and other African countries)

stages.name: Pre-screening questionnaire
stages.what_happens: Short first questions after you apply.

stages.name: Online assessment
stages.what_happens: An online test.

stages.name: Video and/or panel interviews
stages.what_happens: A digital video interview and/or panel interviews with people from the business.

stages.name: Psychometric assessments
stages.what_happens: Detailed tests of ability and working style.

stages.name: Final round
stages.what_happens: A final interview or assessment centre with business leaders.

examples.source_title: Graduate programmes at Standard Bank Group

stages.name: Online cognitive assessments
stages.what_happens: Online thinking and reasoning tests.

stages.name: On-demand video interview
stages.what_happens: You record video answers in your own time to questions chosen for the role.

stages.name: Shortlisting
stages.what_happens: Hiring managers look at the videos and test results together to choose a shortlist.

stages.name: Case study presentation
stages.what_happens: The final stage: you present a case study to the hiring panel.
